title: Praying on earth
hookLine: Shia in the Ja'fari school prostrate on earth, often on a small clay tablet from Karbala

cards: A night of rain in Medina. The mosque's roof is palm branches, and it leaks. At the dawn prayer the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, goes down in prostration onto ground that has turned to mud.
The Companion Abu Sa'id al-Khudri says that afterward he saw the trace of mud and water on the Prophet's forehead. The report sits in Sahih al-Bukhari. Keep that forehead in mind.
Today is about what it touches.

teach.b: Day 901 met the turbah in passing; here's the fuller story. The word means soil, earth, and here, a small object.

teach.h: EARTH, OR WHAT GROWS FROM IT.
teach.b: In the Ja'fari school, the forehead in prostration has to rest on the earth itself, or on something that grows from the earth, as long as it isn't eaten or worn. Bare ground, stone, sand, a mat woven of palm leaves: yes.

A wool carpet, a cotton cloth: not for the forehead. So in a carpeted mosque or a living room, you bring a little earth with you: a small tablet of baked clay, round or square, set where the forehead will land.
Some are plain clay. Some are pressed from the soil of Karbala, where the Prophet's grandson, Imam Husayn, was killed, and they carry that memory into every prayer.
A turbah is not something prayed to. It's something prayed on. The prostration is to God; the clay is only what the forehead touches.

Shia jurists point to the Prophet's own practice, the mud on his forehead, and to the report, also in Sahih al-Bukhari, that the earth has been made for him a place of prayer and a means of purification.
They cite reports from the Imams as well. Sunni schools read the evidence differently.

They allow prostration on a carpet or cloth, citing, among other reports, Companions who spread part of their garment and prostrated on it in fierce heat. Shia jurists read that as an allowance for need.
Both sides share the same scene: the highest part of the body lowered to the ground. They differ on what may lie between.

how: Shia Muslims who follow the Ja'fari school prostrate on earth or on what grows from it, often placing a small clay tablet, a turbah, sometimes made from the soil of Karbala, where the forehead rests.

o: a sacred clay object that Shia Muslims pray toward
a small clay tablet the forehead rests on in prayer
the prayer rug that covers the floor of a mosque

games.q: you follow the Ja'fari school and you're about to pray in a carpeted living room. where does your forehead go?
o: onto a small clay tablet set on the carpet.
games.why: onto the turbah. carpet and cloth aren't earth, and don't grow from it; baked clay is earth you can carry.

practice: If you can, find some clean earth, a plant pot, a stone on the windowsill, even a plain clay mug, and rest your fingertips on it, noticing its temperature, its grain, whether it's damp or dry.

If there's none nearby, rest your palm flat on the floor and picture the soil somewhere underneath, the lowest thing in the room, met on purpose. If you pray, you can remember the One the forehead bows to.

wordCard.voice: Turbah. Soil, earth: the small clay tablet a Ja'fari Shia worshiper sets down so the forehead meets earth in prostration. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: soil, earth; for Shia, the small clay tablet used in prostration.

carryVoice: Your line: forehead on earth. The clay tablet is the Ja'fari answer: earth, and nothing else. See you tomorrow.
